revised_text: A data owner may need to demonstrate that public cluster centers give a reported assignment cost on private records. Examples include an analyst checking a deployed model on sensitive embeddings and an auditor requesting costs for several proposed model updates. Zero-knowledge proofs establish the specified computation without disclosing its private witness \cite{gmr1991knowledge,groth2016}. The difficulty is repeated high-dimensional arithmetic: a direct nearest-center audit evaluates distances in $d$ dimensions for every record and every candidate center. In our Groth16 implementation, a batch of eight 784-dimensional MNIST records requires 1.31 million constraints and 18.5 seconds of proving.

\tpexplain{Paragraph 2 --- quantify the bottleneck. Explain why distances in dimension d are expensive and distinguish native computation from proving cost. Insert a motivating profile from the implemented backend.}
The difficulty is proof cost. For $n$ points, $k$ candidate centroids, and dimension $d$, one assignment step already evaluates $\Theta(nkd)$ coordinate contributions. A ZK circuit must also constrain ranges, compare distances, and materialize witnesses, so fast native linear algebra does not imply a cheap proof \cite{zkcnn2021,ezdps2023}. Whether distance and comparison gadgets dominate in the selected backend is therefore measured rather than assumed.

revised_text: The same committed records can be queried many times. This motivates a two-stage construction. Stage~1 proves once that compact statistics were derived correctly from every committed original row. Stage~2 authenticates the requested statistics and proves nearest-center assignments and their aggregate cost. The central systems question is which statistics allow useful later queries while avoiding repeated original-space work.

revised_text: For one fixed center set, the geometry is elementary. An orthonormal basis spanning the center differences preserves all assignment comparisons; adding each record's squared residual norm recovers every center distance. This follows from Pythagoras and belongs to the established projection-plus-offset approach to clustering sketches \cite{feldman2013tiny,feldman2020tiny,cohen2015dimensionality}. We use this identity as an interface to a proof system. We do not propose a new dimensionality-reduction identity or a new coreset theorem.

\tpexplain{Paragraph 3 --- introduce JL but immediately expose the security subtlety. The novelty setup is commit first, sample second.}
A Johnson--Lindenstrauss (JL) transform maps points from $\mathbb{R}^d$ to $\mathbb{R}^m$, with $m\ll d$, while approximately preserving pairwise distances \cite{johnson1984extensions,achlioptas2003database,kane2014sparser}. This suggests reducing the dimension before proving repeated distance computations. The usual JL guarantee, however, fixes the point set before drawing an independent transform. A prover that sees the transform first can instead choose data in its kernel or in a badly distorted subspace. The protocol order must match the order assumed in the geometric argument.

revised_text: Fixed-center answers alone are insufficient to justify a reusable representation. A stronger task-specific baseline computes and proves the exact winning center and minimum cost in Stage~1, then authenticates those two values in later subset queries. It is cheaper for a single fixed center set. Exact affine scores provide another compact baseline with the same fixed-center information. Both measured implementations specialize preprocessing to the selected centers, so their Stage~1 work is repeated when those centers change.

\tpexplain{One paragraph on classical JL, one on clustering-specific projection dimensions. State theorem parameters accurately and separate pairwise preservation from objective preservation.}
Classical JL embeddings preserve all pairwise distances in a fixed set with target dimension logarithmic in the set size and quadratic in the inverse distortion \cite{johnson1984extensions}. Sparse constructions reduce application time while retaining similar embedding guarantees \cite{kane2014sparser}. Clustering-specific analyses can require dimension depending on $k$ and $\epsilon$ rather than directly on $n$ \cite{cohen2015dimensionality,makarychev2019performance}. Our design uses these results as mathematical interfaces, but does not apply their bounds until the implemented distribution satisfies the cited hypotheses.

revised_text: We therefore study audits under changing public centers. We augment the deployed-center span with principal components of training residuals, and store the resulting head coordinates and residual energy. New centers enter Stage~2 through public head coordinates and residual offsets. They change the query inputs without changing the catalog or the query setup. This yields an exact real-arithmetic distance when the new centers remain in the represented affine span, and an approximation otherwise. The approximation drops a residual cross term, which we expose explicitly and evaluate against original-space distances.

The contribution has three parts:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*]
\item A checked integer, original-data-bound implementation of head and energy statistics, with all-row Stage~1 coverage and authenticated subset queries.
\item A reusable nearest-center circuit with public new-center statistics and a proved sum of compressed assignment margins. One setup serves center sets of the same shape; the margin is a diagnostic, not an original-space certificate.
\item Matched native and actual-proof measurements, including cached exact answers, affine scores, PCA with energy, direct Full proofs, and sparse-JL controls. Across three 64-/256-row proof workloads, reuse crosses the tested center-specific cached baseline at the second center set and reduces ten-set cumulative measured-component cost by factors of 6.82--7.76. Learned head and PCA with energy have similar proof cost; the learned head has higher assignment agreement on these proof catalogs. A separate eight-corpus, five-start campaign checks fixed-center fidelity.
\end{enumerate}

revised_text: Classical head coordinates and residual energy provide a compact interface for verifiable center-based audits. Across the completed 64-/256-row MNIST and 64-row CIFAR-embedding workloads, reuse beats the tested center-specific cached baseline from the second center set and reduces ten-set cumulative measured-component cost by factors of 6.82--7.76. Let real input coordinates be scaled by $S$ and rounded to integers with per-coordinate error at most $1/(2S)$. Hence $\|x-\widetilde x/S\|_2\le\sqrt d/(2S)$; for a pair $u,v$, the distance perturbation is at most $\sqrt d/S$, and the squared-distance error is at most $2\|u-v\|_2\sqrt d/S+d/S^2$. If $|x_t|,|c_t|\le B$, distinct rows within each column imply that a fixed output row receives at most one contribution per input coordinate. Thus a projected point--centroid coordinate has magnitude at most $2dB$, independent of $q$. Put $D_{\max}=4md^2B^2$ and $\Psi_{\max}=nD_{\max}$. Comparison differences may reach $2D_{\max}$. The implementation range-checks signed values against $M=\max\{2dB,2D_{\max},\Psi_{\max}\}$ and requires $p>2M$; tighter data-dependent bounds may improve performance but cannot replace a proved worst-case certificate.

We consider three challenge sources: a verifier nonce, a public randomness beacon referenced by round, and a two-party commit--reveal coin flip. Deriving the seed from $C_X$ alone is deterministic and permits offline search over commitment randomness. The primary protocol therefore uses a fresh 256-bit verifier nonce after $(C_X,C_\theta)$ has entered the task log. A beacon with a commitment deadline gives the cleanest public enforcement, while commit--reveal avoids trusting either party as the sole entropy source.
